clue.text: Lovely lady more fabled when bare (8)

indicators.note: a bare body has had its covering taken off, so each word here loses the letters that clothe it at either end

blocks.note: lADy with its outside letters taken off
mORe stripped down to its middle pair
fABLEd loses the f at the front and the d at the back

explanation.walkthrough: One instruction is doing the same job three times over, which is what lets the sentence read as praise for a lady rather than as an order.
explanation.definitionFit: Lovely and adorable are both everyday adjectives of warm approval, the second being the one you reach for about a child or a puppy.

clue.text: Supremo's order to a curate finally cancelled (8)

indicators.note: to order a shelf is to put its contents into a fresh arrangement, and that is what happens to this handful of letters
the last thing in the word before it is struck out, so that word arrives one letter shorter

blocks.note: the two small words go into the mix exactly as they stand
CURATE with its closing E struck out

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a boss barking an instruction; the wordplay wants 'order' in the other sense, the one a librarian means.
explanation.definitionFit: A supremo is the one person in sole charge, and an autocrat is exactly a ruler who answers to nobody else.

clue.text: Trace very old chopped ham (7)

indicators.note: food that has been through a knife ends up in pieces with no arrangement left to it, and so do these letters

blocks.note: the word itself is the raw material
V is the standard short form of very
O is old in the abbreviation book, as in OE for Old English

explanation.walkthrough: Everything before the definition reads like a shopping list — trace amounts, aged, diced — and none of it is about food at all.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Ham' is theatre slang for playing a part far too broadly, and as a verb it is what a bad actor does on stage.

clue.text: School organisation cycling to get fit (3)

indicators.note: a wheel keeps every spoke in the same order and simply brings a different one to the top, and these three letters rotate the same way

blocks.note: the PTA, the parent-teacher association every school has

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has the committee out on a bike to keep in shape, while the wordplay only wants its initials rolled round one place.
explanation.definitionFit: Apt means well suited to the case, the same sense as a remark that fits an occasion exactly.

clue.text: Part from grille a vent covers (5)

indicators.note: what a cover does is lie over a thing and keep it out of sight, and these words are lying over the letters wanted

blocks.note: the run starts inside grilLE and finishes in A VEnt

explanation.walkthrough: The airbrick in the surface is there to hide a join: the letters straddle the gap between two words, which is where the eye slides past them.
explanation.definitionFit: To part from somebody is to go away from them, the phrasal sense of 'part' rather than the one that means to divide.

clue.text: A surge in activity catches learner out (6)

indicators.note: a catch closes round whatever it has taken, so the letter caught here ends up held in the middle rather than tacked on

blocks.note: the clue's opening word joins in as a single letter
a boom is a sudden rush of growth or business
L is the plate a learner driver carries

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a business report, with a boom and a learner sent packing, and none of it survives into an answer that is about flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: Of a plant, 'out' means in flower — the gardener's sense, not the one about being outside or being dismissed.

clue.text: Cockney chap was flipping covered in pearly tat, maybe being a nuisance (11)

indicators.note: on the surface it is the mild swear word, but to flip a pancake is to land it the other way up, and this piece lands written the other way round
whatever you are covered in goes over you on both sides, so one word here wraps right round the rest

blocks.note: a Cockney drops the aitch, so 'he' comes out as 'e
he was is he LIVED, and that word turned round is the fiend
bling is showy jewellery, and pearls are one example of it — 'maybe' flags the example

explanation.walkthrough: Pearly kings and queens are Cockneys themselves, so the sentence hangs together beautifully while each of its words quietly does a different job.
explanation.definitionFit: To bedevil somebody is to plague or torment them, so the participle names the act of being a persistent pest.

clue.text: Took too much on at once, ultimately (7)

indicators.note: the ultimate item in a queue is the final one, so it is the closing letter of the word before that is wanted

blocks.note: a row on money is a row over money — the two prepositions swap freely
the little word is dropped in whole
the closing letter of oncE

explanation.walkthrough: 'On' for 'over' looks unfair until you try the pair in a sentence: an argument on pay is an argument over pay.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the past tense of overeat, and taking too much at table is precisely what that verb describes.

clue.text: Attack using half of bullets, perhaps, in case (6)

indicators.note: a thing cut in half leaves two equal parts, and only one of them — here the back one — carries into the answer

blocks.note: bullets are an example of AMMO, and the back half of that is MO
lest means in case, as in 'lest we forget'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' flags that bullets are only one example of what is wanted, and 'in case' is a whole phrase rather than the insertion instruction it looks like.
explanation.definitionFit: To molest is to assault or interfere with somebody, and the older, milder sense of pestering is the one that makes 'attack' fair.

clue.text: Most of religious community let down disciple (8)

indicators.note: most of a thing is all but a scrap of it, so the word gives up its final letter and keeps the rest

blocks.note: a religious community is a FOLD, and most of it is FOL
to let a bucket down a well is to lower it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Let down' is doing its literal work here — lowering on a rope, not disappointing — and that swap is what the surface is banking on.
explanation.definitionFit: A disciple is somebody who follows a teacher or a creed, so the two words are plain synonyms in the religious sense.

clue.text: Negotiate withdrawal after soldiers go AWOL (5)

indicators.note: a soldier absent without leave is simply not there any more, and neither are the two letters that stand for him

blocks.note: a withdrawal of troops is a retreat
RE is the Royal Engineers, the crossword's standing army

explanation.walkthrough: The letters that march off are the army's own, which is the joke: no retreat is possible once the soldiers have already gone.
explanation.definitionFit: To treat with an enemy is to parley or bargain with them, the sense kept alive in 'treaty' and rarely met outside crosswords.

clue.text: Much value for money (1,4,4)

blocks.note: the quantity idiom meaning a large amount, as in 'a lot of trouble' or 'considerably older'
the shopper's sense: a bargain is a deal that is good

explanation.walkthrough: Four words and no seam to look for: the whole clue is one phrase read twice, once about quantity and once about buying.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the amount idiom, a good deal of something; the other is a bargain, where deal keeps its trading meaning.

clue.text: Within enclosed chamber, metres inside, tie down stateside digging equipment (9)

indicators.note: what is within a room sits in the middle of it, so everything the clue goes on to name is put into the small space first mentioned
the measurement is not laid beside the rope but in the thick of it, splitting the word it lands in

blocks.note: a cell is a small shut room
to lash a load down is to tie it fast
m is the symbol for metres

explanation.walkthrough: Two insertions, one nested in the other, which is why the clue reads like a stack of orders; 'stateside' is the warning that this bucket is American usage.
explanation.definitionFit: In the US a clamshell is the hinged bucket on a crane, jaws that bite shut like the shellfish it is named after.

clue.text: Drug users mistakenly freed in talks (5,6)

indicators.note: doing a thing mistakenly is getting it into the wrong arrangement, and letters put down wrongly are letters waiting to be sorted

blocks.note: the word goes into the mix as it stands
talks and speaks are the same verb in the same person

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a courtroom, with prisoners let go after negotiations, and 'talks' has to become a synonym before any of its letters are useful.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Speed' is street slang for amphetamines and a freak is a devotee, so the phrase names habitual takers of one particular drug.

clue.text: By means of leaks, drained bottles (5)

indicators.note: a drained glass has nothing left in the middle of it, so the word keeps only the letters standing at its two ends

blocks.note: via means by way of — travelling via Paris
the outside letters of LeakS

explanation.walkthrough: Small glass bottles for medicine are what is wanted, not wine bottles; the leak in the surface is there to make 'drained' look like scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: A vial is a little glass bottle for a medicine or a sample, so the definition is a plain synonym kept in the plural.

clue.text: Direct reorganisation of Welsh factories (2,3,4,5)

indicators.note: a reorganisation keeps the same staff and moves every one of them to a new place, which is the treatment these letters get

blocks.note: the fourteen letters of the two words are the whole of the raw material

explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration is the way in: fourteen letters are too many to shuffle by eye, so let 2,3,4,5 suggest the shape of the phrase first.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means by the straightest possible route, ignoring roads, so it does the work of the adverb 'direct' in 'fly direct'.

clue.text: Borne up bed of glacier, suffering climbing injury (4,4)

indicators.note: a body in pain has nothing where it should be, and letters described as suffering will not stay in the order they were given
a glacier's bed is the rock at the very bottom of it, and in a down clue the bottom of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: both words go into the mix as plain letters
the bottom letter of glacieR

explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'climbing' looks exactly like an instruction to write something upwards, and here it belongs to the definition instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Friction from a rope running through the hands scorches the skin, so the phrase names a mountaineer's hazard by its cause.

clue.text: Piece of paper? (4,4)

blocks.note: the surface offers a sheet or a scrap you could write on, and that is the picture to get out of your head
in a newsroom a piece is an article — the thing a reporter files
the paper is the daily one, so the pieces in it are the stories it prints

explanation.walkthrough: There is no fodder to find and nothing to take apart: the whole clue is one description read two ways, and the question mark is the setter owning up.
explanation.definitionFit: A 'piece' is journalists' word for an article and 'paper' is the daily it appears in, so the phrase reads straight in both trades.

clue.text: Crazily, Trump worsened international speed of data capture (5,3,6)

indicators.note: somebody behaving crazily does things in no sensible sequence, and letters handled that way come out in a new one

blocks.note: the thirteen letters of the two words are the fodder
I is the standard abbreviation for international

explanation.walkthrough: 'Data capture' is the office phrase for getting text into a computer, and typing has been timed this way since the typewriter.
explanation.definitionFit: Typing is data capture, and its rate is quoted as how many words a typist gets down in sixty seconds.

clue.text: One facing problem, weighed down by work (7)

indicators.note: whatever is weighed down by a thing has that thing sitting on top of it, and in a down clue on top means earlier in the answer

blocks.note: OP is a composer's opus, the crossword's standard short 'work'
a poser is a question that stumps you

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an overworked employee with a problem, and the answer has nothing to do with tiredness — 'work' is doing an abbreviation's job.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoever opposes you stands against you, and 'facing' carries the sense of confronting somebody rather than merely looking towards them.

clue.text: Wrong turn oddly heralds finish of economic improvement (7)

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters are the ones wanted — first, third and so on — rather than the whole word
a herald goes ahead to announce what is coming, so these letters are placed in front of what follows them

blocks.note: when something is up, something is wrong — 'what's up?'
the first and third letters of TuRn
the end of anything is its finish

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong' for UP is the best trick here — it is the 'something's up' sense, not the direction, which a down entry makes very tempting.
explanation.definitionFit: Markets are said to be in an uptrend while the graph keeps climbing, so the word is an analyst's name for things getting better.

clue.text: A bit raunchy? I show embarrassment outwardly (6)

indicators.note: what shows outwardly is on the outside, so the long word goes round the single letter instead of standing next to it

blocks.note: the pronoun is taken as the letter it is written with
to blush is to show embarrassment in the face

explanation.walkthrough: Blue is the colour of the smutty joke, so a shade of it is a shade of rudeness, which is the sense the definition is after.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue is the long-standing word for near-the-knuckle comedy, and the -ish ending makes it mildly so rather than outright.

clue.text: Charitable person accommodates pariah (5)

indicators.note: to accommodate somebody is to make room for them inside your own place, and these two words have made room between them

blocks.note: the run bridges charitabLE and PERson

explanation.walkthrough: A charitable person is exactly who would take one in, so surface and mechanism agree for once — which is what makes the join so hard to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: A pariah is an outcast, and the leper is the historic figure of exclusion, the word still thrown at anyone a group shuns.

clue.text: Big US donor's attendance restricted by what he calls checks (4,5)

indicators.note: a thing restricted by something is hemmed in on both sides by it, so one word here is trapped in the middle of the other

blocks.note: the gate is the crowd counted through the turnstiles at a match
an American asks the waiter for the check where a Briton asks for the bill

explanation.walkthrough: 'Big US donor' names one man rather than a type, and the 'he' in the wordplay quietly confirms that a person is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: The Microsoft founder has given away more of his fortune than any other private American, so the description points at one particular philanthropist.

clue.text: Trees in locations bisected by motorway (5)

indicators.note: to bisect a thing is to cut it into two halves, and the cut leaves a gap for whatever made it

blocks.note: where a thing lies is where it is — the lie of the land
M is the prefix on every British motorway number

explanation.walkthrough: These are the tall avenue trees of a park, not the fruit, which is how the clue gets away with an unqualified 'trees'.
explanation.definitionFit: The lime, or linden, is a broad-leaved avenue tree, so the plural defines by example rather than by synonym.

clue.text: Platform One at northern station - note crush (9)

blocks.note: one is the Roman numeral I
N is the compass abbreviation for northern
STA is how a timetable shortens station
G is a note of the musical scale
to ram is to force or crush together

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a railway announcement built out of the abbreviations a timetable really uses, which is why a very modern answer hides so well in it.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Platform' is the current word for a place online where people publish, so the photo-sharing app is one and the railway sense is a decoy.

clue.text: That's the thing about poor grades, son (2,3)

indicators.note: words written about a subject go all the way round it, so the short word opens up and takes the rest inside

blocks.note: 'the thing' is simply it
a D and an E are the poor marks on a school report
s is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.walkthrough: Latin, and the enumeration 2,3 is the tell: two short words, which in English we usually write as the abbreviation i.e.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin means literally 'that is', the words i.e. stands for, so it substitutes for the contraction word for word.

clue.text: Reportedly, you can get down from this mountain (3)

indicators.note: a report hands you the words as they were heard rather than as they were written, so the sound is what matters and the spelling is not

blocks.clueFragment: you can get down from this
blocks.note: the bird whose breast feathers make eiderdown is the eider, and saying that name gives the peak

explanation.walkthrough: Mount Ida overlooks Crete, and the 'down' of the clue is a duck's soft under-feathers rather than a direction of travel.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount Ida is the Cretan peak where Zeus was said to have been raised, so a bare 'mountain' is pointing at a proper name.

clue.text: Fergie returns to confront start of soccer trouble (6)

indicators.note: to return is to come back along the way you went, so the name is written out in the opposite direction
the start of a word is the letter it opens with, and that single letter is all that is taken

blocks.note: Fergie is Sarah Ferguson, and SARAH comes back the other way
the opening letter of Soccer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fergie' is two people on the sports pages, the Duchess and the football manager, and the soccer in the surface points firmly at the wrong one.
explanation.definitionFit: To harass somebody is to trouble them again and again, taking 'trouble' as the verb meaning to pester rather than to worry.

clue.text: First man to bring in flier for viewing African landmark (5,3)

indicators.note: to bring a guest in is to fetch them inside the house, so this piece ends up in the middle of the other one

blocks.note: Adam is the first man of Genesis
a swan is heavy but a perfectly good flier

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a holiday snapshot, complete with a leaflet, and that is what makes the biblical reading so easy to walk past.
explanation.definitionFit: The great dam across the Nile in southern Egypt is among the continent's best-known structures, so the phrase names it by example.
